title: Where the cable ran out at 'Cemetery'

place.label: California Street at Presidio Avenue (formerly Central Avenue, nicknamed 'Cemetery')

hook: In 1880 two cable car lines ended at Central Avenue, a stop riders called "Cemetery." From there, smoky steam trains carried them on west.
story: Presidio Avenue used to be called Central Avenue, and riders knew the stop as "Cemetery" [1]. The California Street Cable Railroad began running cable cars from Kearny Street to Central Avenue on May 30, 1879. Its franchise ran on to First Avenue (today's Arguello), and for that last stretch it was allowed to use steam. So the company leased a Southern Pacific locomotive and one car, and they started running from Cemetery Avenue on February 6, 1880. The steam train probably lasted until about 1884. After that a one-horse car took over [1]. A few blocks south, the Geary Street, Park & Ocean Railroad opened on February 16, 1880. Its cable passengers also changed at Central Avenue, onto four Baldwin steam dummies that ran on to Golden Gate Park [1]. The spot was a gateway even before the cable. An 1860s photograph shows a tollhouse on Point Lobos Road, now Geary, near Presidio Avenue, with Calvary Cemetery's graves behind it [2]. By 1890 the Point Lobos Improvement Club was calling the steam dummy a "noisy, sooty and smoky nuisance." Full cable service on the Geary line, from Market Street to Golden Gate Park, opened on August 7, 1892 [1].

title: A soldiers' hospital on Jordan's sandlots

place.label: Jordan Park (blocks between Geary Blvd, California St, Palm Ave and Commonwealth Ave)

hook: Before Jordan Park had lawns and wide streets, it had rows of tents, a crowded field hospital and volunteer soldiers waiting for ships to the Philippines.
story: In May 1898, with the Spanish-American War under way, volunteer regiments poured into San Francisco on their way to the Philippines. Thousands camped in the Richmond at Camp Merritt [1]. When the number of soldiers there neared 7,000, the Army spread onto James Clark Jordan's land next door, today's Jordan Park. On May 28 the division hospital moved here. Troops from Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota and Iowa pitched tents on the blocks between Geary Boulevard, California Street, Palm Avenue and Commonwealth Avenue [1]. Sand, fog, thin cotton blankets and poor sanitation made men sick. On July 11 more than 150 soldiers crowded the field hospital, a number of them with pneumonia. Ten men died that summer of measles, typhoid and other diseases. Joseph I. Markey of the 51st Iowa wrote that he hoped "the guilty will not go unpunished" [1]. By August the Army had moved the remaining troops back to the Presidio [1]. Jordan had bought these blocks in 1891. Between 1900 and 1920 he developed them into a district of wide streets and large houses set on spacious lots with lawns and gardens [2].

title: The homeopaths build a college at Maple Street

place.label: Corner of Sacramento and Maple Streets (site of Hahnemann Hospital College; hospital later on California Street)

hook: A contractor who refused to take a dollar, a 2,000-book library and women on the faculty: San Francisco's homeopathic medical school finally got its own home in 1899.
story: San Francisco's homeopathic doctors ran their own medical college, named for Samuel Hahnemann, the founder of homeopathy. Early in 1895 its trustees picked a lot at the corner of Sacramento and Maple Streets [1]. Doctors from Oakland to Carson, Nevada chipped in, and the college raised just over $10,000. The contractor, George Lang, was a keen homeopath and refused to take a single dollar for himself [1]. The cornerstone went down on February 4, 1899, and the building was dedicated on July 25 with Mayor Phelan among the speakers. It was a colonial-style building of four floors, and gold letters over the porch read "Hahnemann Hospital College." Inside were a chemistry laboratory, a museum and more than 2,000 volumes collected by Samuel Lilienthal and his son James [1]. Women were on the faculty: Florence N. Ward was professor of obstetrics, and her husband, the dean James W. Ward, taught diseases of women [1]. The cornerstone of a Hahnemann Hospital was laid on May 31, 1905 [1]. It stood on California Street next to Children's Hospital and was damaged in the 1906 earthquake. In 1970 it was renamed Marshall Hale Hospital and later became part of California Pacific Medical Center [2].

title: The Elite, the Rex, the Plaza, the Vogue
hook: A little neighbourhood cinema has gone through four names and more than a century. In 2007 it was feared lost; in 2025 it got its neon back.
story: The small cinema at 3290 Sacramento Street is one of the city's oldest. Sources disagree on when it opened. Cinema Treasures says it opened as the Elite Theatre in 1910. Its current operator says it was established in 1912 [1][3]. It was renamed the Rex in 1919 and was the Plaza by 1932. On July 1, 1938 it reopened as the Vogue, with Katharine Hepburn in Bringing Up Baby and Jack Holt in Under Suspicion. The Blumenfeld circuit ran it then. United Artists ran it later [1]. Cinema Treasures lists Simeon Charles Lee as architect, and its style as Streamline Moderne [1]. In 2007 the Vogue closed for a short while, and people feared it would be torn down. Instead a small non-profit bought it and volunteers reopened it [2]. Today the San Francisco Neighborhood Theater Foundation owns it and the non-profit CinemaSFBay runs it [3]. On December 3, 2025 Mayor Daniel Lurie cut the ribbon and lit its restored marquee. Neon Works had spent five months on it, replacing the transformers and reusing some of the original tubes. Afterwards everyone was invited to stay for a free screening of the 1936 film San Francisco [3][4].

title: Muni's first car house, cut by a cemetery

place.label: Presidio Division (Geary Car House), 949 Presidio Avenue at Geary Boulevard

hook: America's first big-city public transit system was run for nearly a century from a car barn with one corner lopped off, because a graveyard was in the way.
story: In 1912 the new Municipal Railway built its Geary Car House at Geary and Presidio Avenue. It was a reinforced-concrete building on bedrock, with streetcar shops, storage tracks, a three-storey office tower and an Art Deco relief over the bronze doors at 949 Presidio Avenue [1]. Its neighbours were the dead: Laurel Hill Cemetery lay to the north and Calvary Cemetery across Geary. The building's northeast corner had to be cut at an odd angle to fit the edge of Laurel Hill, and the clipped corner can still be seen beside the bus-yard entrance [2]. The cemeteries also blocked streets. Bush and Post dead-ended at Laurel Hill, and business owners had to settle for a short jog linking Bush with Masonic [3]. After Laurel Hill's graves went to Colma, Muni dug a trolley-bus yard in the late 1940s right on top of the old cemetery ground, and the building became Presidio Division [1][2]. The streetcar bays along Geary were once used to store the city's voting machines. The building was Muni's headquarters until the early 2000s. It is now Muni's oldest bus yard, and SFMTA plans to rebuild it [1].

title: An empire's enemies on Wood Street

place.label: Ghadar Memorial (Gadar Memorial Hall), 5 Wood Street

hook: On a short street above Geary, Indian revolutionaries ran their headquarters and printing press, working to overthrow British rule a world away.
story: The Ghadar Party was founded in San Francisco in 1913 to free India from British rule by force. Most of its members were South Asian workers on the West Coast [1][2]. Its weekly paper, Ghadar, first came out in November 1913. Its masthead called itself "an enemy of British rule" [1]. The party began at 436 Hill Street, active there from 1913 to 1917, and then moved its headquarters to 5 Wood Street [2]. The three-storey house there held a printing press and people living and working together, and it hosted public and secret meetings [2]. In August 1914 the party called on overseas Indians to go home and rise up, and some 8,000 were said to have gone. Because of strong British vigilance, most were captured on the way or when they arrived [2]. The Hindu-German Conspiracy Trial that followed in San Francisco broke up what was left of the leadership. In the courtroom one defendant, Ram Singh, shot the party leader Ram Chandra dead [1]. After independence the building passed to the Government of India, formally in 1952. Ground was broken in September 1974 and the memorial opened in March 1975 [2]. The consulate calls that work a restoration, but FoundSF says the present building went up after the original was demolished [1][2].

title: A redwood hall for the Campfire Girls

place.label: Campfire Girls Building (Campfire Golden Gate Council Headquarters), 325 Arguello Boulevard

hook: A student of Bernard Maybeck gave a girls' club a Bay Area Craftsman clubhouse, with redwood trusses vaulting over its meeting hall.
story: In 1929 the Campfire Girls Association Building went up on Arguello Boulevard between California and Clement. Its architect was Henry Gutterson [1]. The city's landmark report calls it a significant example of the Bay Area Craftsman style, with picturesque, irregular massing [1]. Inside, redwood was used for the trim, panelling and beams, and the "central meeting hall" rises into trussed cathedral vaults [1]. Gutterson was one of the second generation of Bay Area architects who followed Bernard Maybeck, Ernest Coxhead, Willis Polk and A. Page Brown. He had studied under Maybeck at Berkeley and worked with him on buildings including the First Church of Christ, Scientist in Berkeley. He also designed more than thirty houses in St. Francis Wood [1]. The City Planning Commission recommended it for landmark status in February 1984 [1]. It became San Francisco Landmark No. 169 on June 30, 1984 [2].

title: A cinema named for the new bridge

place.label: Bridge Theatre, 3010 Geary Boulevard at Blake Street

hook: It opened in 1939 as a cut-price, late-run neighbourhood house, then spent over half a century as one of the city's great art cinemas.
story: Attilio A. Zerga built the New Bridge on Geary at Blake Street. It opened in July 1939 with Irene Dunne and Charles Boyer in Love Affair [1]. The theatre historian Jack Tillmany gives July 21, and Cinema Treasures July 22 [1][2]. The name honoured the Golden Gate Bridge, which had opened in 1937 [1]. Until the mid-1950s it was a cheap, late-run neighbourhood theatre. Films reached it after Market Street and the second-run houses, so Love Affair was three or four months old when it played here [1]. In the mid-1950s the Bridge became an exclusive first-run "art" house for prestige American and foreign films, and it did well at it for decades [1]. Cinema Treasures calls it one of the most successful venues for independent and foreign film in San Francisco. It had 399 seats [2]. Its last operator, Landmark Theatres, closed it on December 27, 2012 after The Perks of Being a Wallflower [1]. The building was renovated with its facade and blade sign kept, and it reopened as the San Francisco Baseball Academy [1].

title: Deli, laundromat and five-and-dime at Laurel Village

place.label: Laurel Village shops, 3401 California Street (California St between Laurel and Spruce)

hook: A 1951 city tax photo shows a strip of butchers, bakers and a Feed Bag diner. Seventy years later only two of its shops were left.
story: In 1951 a city assessor's photographer took pictures along California Street at Laurel Village. At 3401 California they show the Feed Bag Restaurant, Hanken's Delicatessen, Joe Klein's Choice Meats and the Winfield Sage Laundromat [1]. Other storefronts ran west along California: a Danish pastry shop, dry cleaner, hardware store, furniture showroom, beauty salon, supermarket, produce store, liquor store, florist, television store and a real estate and insurance office. There was also a Standard 5 & 10 [1]. A shop called Young Man's Fancy dressed "the younger set" here in Bruce Bary clothes from the end of World War II until the turn of the millennium. The columnist who remembers it notes you don't see many little boys in navy blazers any more [2]. Harold Dobbs, a co-founder of Mel's Drive-In, also co-founded the Red Roof restaurants, one of them on California Street near Laurel Village. Dobbs was a supervisor and ran for mayor in 1963, 1967 and 1971 [3]. Tastes and rents changed. The A.G. Ferrari delicatessen here closed in 2017 [4]. By 2022, of the whole 1951 line-up, only the grocery (now CalMart) and the Standard 5 & 10, partnered with Ace Hardware, were still open [1].

title: The singing rabbi's house for holy hippies

place.label: Former House of Love and Prayer, 347 Arguello Boulevard (between California and Clement)

hook: For $300 a month, a Georgian house on Arguello became a commune where hundreds of young seekers came for Shabbat songs led by Shlomo Carlebach.
story: Shlomo Carlebach, known as "the Singing Rabbi," played the Berkeley Folk Festival in 1966. He invited the crowd to Shabbat that Friday, and about 800 people came [1]. He wanted a place in San Francisco where, in his words, "when you come, someone loves you; when you leave, someone misses you." In April 1968 his follower Aryae Coopersmith rented a large two-storey Georgian house at 347 Arguello Boulevard. The rent was $300 a month, plus a $50 deposit [1]. They called it the House of Love and Prayer. A few people lived there and ran it. It worked as a free hostel during the week, and hundreds came each week for Shabbat, Carlebach's melodies and his teaching [1]. The historian Yaakov Ariel describes its "Hasidic hippies" as a mixture of traditional Hasidic Judaism and the counterculture, a pairing most Jews of the time could not understand. He dates the House from 1967 to 1977 [2]. The Arguello house closed in May 1970, after the group put a down payment on a house at 1456 9th Avenue for a yeshiva. By the mid-1970s the House had become more traditionally Orthodox [1].

title: The subway that wasn't, the underpass that was

place.label: Geary Boulevard underpass at Masonic and Presidio Avenues

hook: Planners once drew BART trains under the Richmond with a stop at Masonic. What the corner got instead was a car tunnel under Geary.
story: Geary Boulevard's fast lanes began in the Western Addition. In the early to mid 1950s the A-1 redevelopment project took homes and businesses by eminent domain and bulldozed them. Its first big job was to widen Geary into an eight-lane expressway, with tunnels under Fillmore Street and under Presidio and Masonic, to speed traffic into the Richmond District [1]. The families and businesses pushed out were scattered, and the cleared land sat empty for years [1]. In September 1961, before the 1962 vote that approved BART, an early plan showed a branch from Montgomery Street deep into the Richmond. It would have had stations at Union Square, Van Ness, Fillmore, Masonic, Arguello, 11th Avenue and 25th Avenue [2]. The branch was never built [2]. At Masonic, the city got the underpass instead. It opened in 1974. A local columnist writes that some would call it just an underpass, but with streets and sidewalks above it, it counts as a tunnel. It removed a major bottleneck between downtown and the Richmond [3].

title: The Coronet's lines for Star Wars

place.label: Site of the Coronet Theatre, 3575 Geary Boulevard at Palm Avenue (now Institute on Aging)

hook: Fox doubted Star Wars, so a booker gave it the Coronet. Lines soon circled the block, and it became the film's top-earning theatre in America.
story: The Coronet opened on Geary on November 2, 1949 with I Was a Male War Bride. It had 1,350 loge-style seats and a room with a television set that patrons could watch for free [1]. From 1956 it was a roadshow house. Oklahoma! ran for 44 weeks, and Around the World in 80 Days for nearly two years [1]. In 1977 20th Century Fox wanted its big theatres for The Other Side of Midnight. The booker Gary Meyer put that film in the smaller Alexandria and gave Star Wars the Coronet, because "I wanted the giant screen" [2]. It opened on May 25, 1977, one of just 32 theatres in the country to do so. The lines were split in two and snaked around the block. Manager Albert Levin saw "old people, young people, children, Hare Krishna groups," with chess players and painted faces [2]. Neighbours on Jordan Avenue couldn't park, and local children sold hot dogs from wagons [2]. The Coronet took $2 million in six months, more than any other Star Wars theatre in the country [2]. It closed on March 17, 2005 and was demolished in 2007 to make way for the Institute on Aging [1][2].
